_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 6 specification: one article, six gaps, SEVEN sentences A–G, one of them extra. Each removed sentence hooks backwards by reference (it, them, this objection, all this effort, the change) and forwards to the next sentence. The extra sentence (C) tempts gap 5 but 'Even so' needs a contrast the text does not give, and the next sentence must describe what people saw. Used by the Part 6 practice page and by Full test 2.
title: The night the lights went out
subtitle: A retired teacher persuaded a small town to switch off its streetlights for two hours. Nobody expected what happened next.
text: When Hannah Reid moved to the small town of Kilbrae, she noticed something odd on her first clear night. Standing in her garden, she could see the Milky Way stretching right across the sky, something she had not seen since she was a child. {1} By the time she reached the main square, it had disappeared altogether, hidden behind the orange glow of the streetlights.

Hannah, a retired physics teacher, decided to find out why. She discovered that Kilbrae had more than four hundred streetlights for a population of under three thousand, and that most of them stayed on all night, lighting empty roads. She spent several evenings walking around with a notebook, recording where each light was and which way it faced. {2} She took her figures to the next meeting of the town council.

The councillors listened politely but were not convinced. Switching off the lights, they argued, would make people feel unsafe, and there would certainly be complaints. {3} Instead, she suggested a single experiment: for one night in October, every light in the town would be turned off between ten o'clock and midnight. If it went badly, she promised, she would never raise the subject again.

To her surprise, the council agreed. Hannah spent the following weeks persuading shops, cafés and households to join in, and borrowing telescopes from every amateur astronomer she could find. The local school agreed to provide hot drinks, and a farmer offered a field for parking. {4} When the evening came, however, more than six hundred people gathered on the football pitch at the edge of town.

At ten o'clock the lights went out. For a moment there was silence, and then a long, collective gasp. {5} Children who had never seen a shooting star counted eleven in the first hour, shouting each one out to their parents, and the queues for the telescopes stretched halfway across the pitch. One farmer, who had lived in Kilbrae all his life, said he had had no idea the sky had so much in it.

The evening was such a success that the council has since replaced the old streetlights with new ones that point downwards and dim automatically after midnight. Residents say the streets feel no less safe than before, and the police report no rise in crime. {6} Kilbrae is now one of a small number of places in the country to be officially recognised as a 'dark-sky town', and visitors arrive every winter simply to look up.
As for the complaints the councillors feared, there have been just two. Both, Hannah points out with some satisfaction, came from people who wanted the lights turned off earlier.
sentences: Privately, though, she feared that all this effort would be for a handful of people.
Yet the further she walked towards the town centre, the fainter it became.
Even so, a few people stayed indoors with their curtains closed.
The change has also cut the town's electricity bill by almost a third.
Hannah had expected this objection and did not try to argue with it.
Above them, thousands of stars had appeared, far more than most of those present had ever seen.
Many of them, she noticed, sent as much light up into the sky as down onto the pavement.
why: 'It' is the Milky Way; 'the further she walked… the fainter' leads to 'By the time she reached the main square, it had disappeared'.
'Them' is the four hundred streetlights; light sent 'up into the sky' is the figure she takes to the council.
'This objection' is the fear that people would feel unsafe; she does not argue but 'Instead' suggests an experiment.
'All this effort' sums up the persuading and borrowing; her fear of 'a handful of people' is answered by 'however, more than six hundred'.
'Them' is the crowd and the stars explain the gasp; the shooting stars then add to what they saw. C cannot follow a gasp of wonder with 'Even so'.
'The change' is the new streetlights; 'also' adds a second benefit before the dark-sky recognition.
